posts.caption:
Income, explained simply 👇

Income is the money you receive, usually from work, a business or investments. It's the starting point of every money plan.

Save this for the next time someone throws finance jargon at you. 🔖

New term every day. Follow @equivisionbasics.

Educational content only, not financial advice.

#income #money #finance #personalfinance #financialliteracy #moneybasics #learnfinance

slides.headline: Income is the money you [[receive]], usually from [[work]] or investments.
slides.footer: It's the starting point of every money plan.

slides.headline: You take a part-time job paying [[$15]] an hour.

steps.title: 20 hours × $15 = $300
steps.sub: That's one week's pay, before tax.

slides.label: WHERE IT COMES FROM
slides.headline: Income has [[many]] forms.
slides.sub: It isn't only a paycheck.

rows.text: Wages or a salary from work
Profit from selling something
Interest and dividends

slides.note: Some income is taxed before it reaches you.

slides.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slides.headline: Income isn't the same as [[wealth]].
slides.sub: Wealth is what you keep, not what you earn.

rows.text: Spend less than you earn: wealth grows

slides.note: Earning a lot and keeping a lot are different things.

slides.title: Income = Money in
slides.sub: Money that comes to you.
checks: It can come from **work or investments**

posts.caption:
Budget, explained simply 👇

A budget is a plan for what you'll do with your money each month. You decide where every dollar goes before you spend it.

Save this for the next time someone throws finance jargon at you. 🔖

New term every day. Follow @equivisionbasics.

Educational content only, not financial advice.

#budget #savingmoney #finance #personalfinance #financialliteracy #moneybasics #learnfinance

slides.headline: A budget is a [[plan]] for what you'll do with your [[money]] each month.
slides.footer: You tell your money where to go.

slides.headline: You earn [[$2,000]] a month. Time to plan.
slides.closing: Every dollar has a job. That's a [[budget]].

slides.label: A POPULAR RULE
slides.headline: Try the [[50/30/20]] rule.
slides.sub: One simple way to split your income.

rows.text: Needs: rent, food, bills
Wants: fun and treats
Savings or paying off debt

slides.note: It's a guideline, not a law. Adjust it to fit your life.

slides.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slides.headline: A budget shows where money [[goes]].
slides.sub: Most people are surprised by their own spending.

rows.text: You spot leaks before they grow
You can afford your goals on purpose
With no plan, money quietly disappears

slides.note: You don't need an app. A notebook works.

slides.title: Budget = A plan
slides.sub: Tell your money where to go.
checks: Plan your **income** before you spend it

slides.headline: Savings is money you [[set aside]] today instead of [[spending]] it.
slides.footer: Saving means spending less than you earn.

steps.title: Your bank may add interest
steps.sub: It pays you to keep money there.

steps.title: It's ready when you need it
steps.sub: A trip, a car, or a surprise bill.

slides.label: A SIMPLE HABIT
slides.headline: Pay [[yourself]] first.

rows.text: Your money arrives
Move some to savings straight away
Spend the rest

slides.label: WHERE TO KEEP IT
slides.headline: Safe and [[easy to reach]].

rows.text: Low risk: the value doesn't swing wildly
Easy to withdraw when you need it

slides.title: Savings = Set aside
slides.sub: Keep some of what you earn.

posts.caption:
Interest, explained simply 👇

Interest is the price of using money. Banks pay it to you when you save, and you pay it to lenders when you borrow.

Save this for the next time someone throws finance jargon at you. 🔖

New term every day. Follow @equivisionbasics.

Educational content only, not financial advice.

#interest #banking #finance #personalfinance #financialliteracy #moneybasics #learnfinance

slides.headline: Interest is the [[price]] of using [[money]].
slides.footer: It works in both directions.

slides.headline: You put [[$1,000]] in a savings account paying 3%.

steps.title: The bank uses your money
steps.sub: It lends it out to others.

slides.label: TWO SIDES
slides.headline: Both directions.
slides.sub: You earn it when you save, and pay it when you borrow.
slides.note: Simple example: one year, nothing added or withdrawn.

slides.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slides.headline: The [[rate]] makes the difference.
slides.sub: A small change in the rate can mean a big change in cost.

rows.text: Saving: a higher rate means you earn more
Borrowing: a higher rate means you pay more

slides.note: Rates change with the economy and differ by lender.

slides.title: Interest = Price of money
slides.sub: Paid to savers, paid by borrowers.
checks: A higher rate means a **bigger amount**

#debt #borrowing #finance #personalfinance #financialliteracy #moneybasics #learnfinance

slides.headline: Debt is money you [[owe]] to someone else and must [[pay back]].

slides.headline: You borrow [[$500]] to fix your laptop.

slides.label: NOT ALL DEBT IS EQUAL
slides.headline: It depends on the [[loan]].
slides.sub: The purpose and the cost both matter.

rows.text: Can help: paying for education or a home
Can hurt: costly debt for things that lose value
Check the interest rate before you borrow

slides.note: General education only. Everyone's situation is different.

slides.label: THE SNOWBALL
slides.headline: Debt can grow.
slides.sub: Unpaid debt gets bigger as interest is added.
slides.note: Example: 20% added yearly, nothing repaid.

slides.title: Debt = Money you owe
slides.sub: Borrow carefully.

posts.caption:
Net worth, explained simply 👇

Net worth is what you own minus what you owe. It's a snapshot of where you stand financially today.

Save this for the next time someone throws finance jargon at you. 🔖

New term every day. Follow @equivisionbasics.

Educational content only, not financial advice.

#networth #wealth #finance #personalfinance #financialliteracy #moneybasics #learnfinance

slides.headline: Net worth is what you [[own]] minus what you [[owe]].
slides.footer: It's a snapshot of where you stand.

slides.headline: Add up what you own, then take away what you owe.

steps.title: You owe $12,000
steps.sub: A student loan and a card balance.

slides.closing: Own minus owe is your [[net worth]].

slides.label: THE GAP
slides.headline: The gap counts.
slides.sub: The difference between the two bars is your net worth.

chart.title: What you own vs what you owe

slides.note: Net worth is negative if you owe more than you own.

slides.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slides.headline: It can [[change]].
slides.sub: Small actions move it in either direction.

rows.text: Pay off debt: net worth rises
Save or invest more: it rises
Borrow more than you build: it falls

slides.note: Check it once or twice a year to see your progress.

slides.title: Net worth = Own - Owe
slides.sub: Your financial snapshot.
checks: Aim to see it **grow** over time

posts.caption:
Emergency fund, explained simply 👇

An emergency fund is money set aside only for surprises, like a car repair or a lost job, so a bad day doesn't turn into debt.

Save this for the next time someone throws finance jargon at you. 🔖

New term every day. Follow @equivisionbasics.

Educational content only, not financial advice.

#emergencyfund #savings #finance #personalfinance #financialliteracy #moneybasics #learnfinance

slides.headline: An emergency fund is a [[cushion]] for [[surprise]] costs.
slides.footer: It keeps a bad day from becoming debt.

slides.headline: Your car breaks down. The repair costs [[$800]].

steps.title: Without a fund
steps.sub: You may borrow and pay interest.

slides.label: HOW MUCH?
slides.headline: How much is [[enough]]?
slides.sub: A common guide: 3 to 6 months of basic costs.
slides.note: Start small. Even $500 helps. Needs differ for everyone.

slides.label: THE RULES
slides.headline: Keep it [[separate]].
slides.sub: Hard to spend by accident, easy to reach in a real emergency.

rows.text: Keep it in a savings account, apart from spending
Spending it on holidays or sales
Keep it out of risky investments

slides.note: Emergencies only: car, medical, or a lost job.

slides.title: Emergency fund = Cushion
slides.sub: For surprises only.
checks: Keep it **safe and easy to reach**

posts.caption:

#creditscore #credit #finance #personalfinance #financialliteracy #moneybasics #learnfinance

slides.headline: A credit score is a [[number]] that shows how [[reliably]] you repay.
slides.footer: A higher score usually means cheaper loans.

slides.headline: Two people ask for the [[same loan]].

steps.title: The lender charges Alex more
steps.sub: Higher risk means a higher rate.

slides.label: WHAT MOVES IT
slides.headline: A few habits [[shape]] it.
slides.sub: The same habits work almost everywhere.

rows.text: Pay every bill on time
Missed payments and maxed-out cards

slides.note: Ranges and rules differ by country.

slides.label: WHY IT MATTERS
slides.headline: It opens [[doors]].
slides.sub: Lenders and landlords often check it.

rows.text: Lower interest rates on loans
Easier to rent or get approved
A low score can mean a no, or higher costs

slides.note: Score names and ranges vary from country to country.

slides.title: Credit score = Trust grade
slides.sub: Your reputation as a borrower.
checks: A number showing **how reliably you repay**

posts.caption:
APR, explained simply 👇

#apr #loans #finance #personalfinance #financialliteracy #moneybasics #learnfinance

slides.headline: APR is the [[yearly cost]] of borrowing, shown as a [[percentage]].
slides.footer: It helps you compare similar loans.

slides.headline: A card charges [[24%]] APR. You owe $1,000.

steps.title: 24% APR is per year
steps.sub: It's the yearly price of borrowing.

slides.closing: That yearly price tag is the [[APR]].

slides.label: COMPARE LOANS
slides.headline: Compare the rate.
slides.sub: Same loan, different APR, different cost.

chart.title: Cost of borrowing $1,000 for a year

slides.note: Simple example: one year, nothing repaid along the way.

slides.label: HOW TO USE IT
slides.headline: Read the [[APR]].

rows.text: A lower APR is cheaper to borrow
A higher APR costs you more
Compare APRs, not just monthly payments

slides.note: What APR includes varies by country and product.

slides.title: APR = Yearly cost
slides.sub: The price of borrowing.
checks: The **yearly cost** of a loan, in %

posts.caption:

posts.caption:
Risk, explained simply 👇

Risk is the chance that things turn out worse than you expected, including losing some or all of your money. Higher potential reward usually comes with higher risk.

Save this for the next time someone throws finance jargon at you. 🔖

New term every day. Follow @equivisionbasics.

Educational content only, not financial advice.

#risk #investing #finance #personalfinance #financialliteracy #moneybasics #learnfinance

slides.headline: Risk is the [[chance]] you lose money or get a [[worse]] result.
slides.footer: Higher possible reward usually means higher risk.

steps.title: A: a savings account
steps.sub: Grows slowly. Low chance of losing money.

steps.title: B: company shares
steps.sub: Could grow more. Could also fall.

steps.title: You choose what you can accept

slides.label: IT'S PERSONAL
slides.headline: Your [[comfort]] level counts.
slides.sub: The right amount of risk differs from person to person.

rows.text: How long until you need the money
How much a loss would hurt you
How you feel when prices fall

slides.note: There is no single right answer for everyone.

slides.label: BOTH SIDES
slides.headline: Risk isn't [[bad]].
slides.sub: But taking none has a cost too.

rows.text: Some risk is how investments can grow
Too much can hurt when you need the cash
Too little: inflation can eat your savings

slides.note: Educational only. Not a recommendation.

slides.title: Risk = Chance of loss
slides.sub: The price of possible reward.
checks: Match it to **your goals and comfort**

slides.label: USE IT WELL

posts.caption:
Liquidity, explained simply 👇

Liquidity is how quickly you can turn something into cash without losing much value. Cash is the most liquid thing there is; a house is not.

Educational content only, not financial advice.

#liquidity #money #finance #personalfinance #financialliteracy #moneybasics #learnfinance

slides.headline: Liquidity is how [[fast]] you can turn something into [[cash]].
slides.footer: Cash is the most liquid thing there is.

slides.headline: You need [[$500]] today. What can you use?

steps.title: Shares
steps.sub: Often a day or two to get cash.

slides.label: A ROUGH RANKING
slides.headline: Fastest to [[slowest]].
slides.sub: Speed depends on the asset and the market.

rows.text: Cash and bank accounts
Shares and funds
Property, art, collectibles

slides.note: A rough guide. Real speed varies.

slides.label: THE TRADE-OFF
slides.headline: Speed can [[cost]] you.
slides.sub: Selling in a hurry may mean a lower price.

steps.title: $500 in a stock
steps.sub: A small piece of a company.

rows.text: See what you own

rows.text: What it's all worth together

posts.caption:

slides.headline: Pros and [[cons]].
slides.sub: Convenience comes at a price.

rows.text: Instant variety from one purchase

posts.caption:
Index fund, explained simply 👇

An index fund copies a market index, such as a list of 500 big companies, instead of trying to beat it. That usually means low fees and wide diversification.

Save this for the next time someone throws finance jargon at you. 🔖

New term every day. Follow @equivisionbasics.

Educational content only, not financial advice.

#indexfund #investing #finance #personalfinance #financialliteracy #moneybasics #learnfinance

slides.headline: An index fund [[copies]] a list of companies instead of trying to [[beat]] it.
slides.footer: It aims to match the market, not beat it.

slides.headline: Say an index follows [[500]] big companies.

steps.title: The index is a scoreboard
steps.sub: It shows how those companies do.

slides.closing: A fund that copies an index is an [[index fund]].

slides.label: WHY PEOPLE LIKE THEM
slides.headline: Simple and [[cheap]].
slides.sub: No expensive manager is picking stocks.

rows.text: Low fees
Spread across many companies
You match the market, you can't beat it

slides.note: Index funds can still fall when markets fall.

slides.label: TWO STYLES
slides.headline: Active vs [[index]].
slides.sub: Two ways to run a fund.

rows.text: A manager tries to beat the market
The fund simply copies the market

slides.note: Many active funds fail to beat their index over long periods.

slides.title: Index fund = Copycat
slides.sub: It follows the market.

posts.caption:
Dollar-cost averaging, explained simply 👇

Dollar-cost averaging means investing the same amount at regular times, whatever the price. You buy more shares when prices are low and fewer when they're high.

Save this for the next time someone throws finance jargon at you. 🔖

New term every day. Follow @equivisionbasics.

Educational content only, not financial advice.

#dollarcostaveraging #investing #finance #personalfinance #financialliteracy #moneybasics #learnfinance

slides.headline: Dollar-cost averaging means investing the [[same amount]] on a [[regular schedule]].
slides.footer: You don't try to guess the perfect moment.

slides.headline: You invest [[$100]] a month, whatever the price.

slides.label: WHAT THE SAME $100 BUYS
slides.headline: Low price, more shares.
slides.sub: The same $100 buys more shares when the price drops.
slides.note: Illustrative numbers only.

slides.label: HONEST LIMITS
slides.headline: It isn't [[magic]].
slides.sub: It's a habit, not a guarantee.

rows.text: Eases the stress of timing the market
Builds a steady investing habit
Doesn't prevent losses in a falling market

slides.note: It can't guarantee a profit. Educational only.

slides.title: DCA = Steady investing
slides.sub: Same amount, regular schedule.
checks: You buy **more** when prices are low

posts.caption:

Save this for the next time someone throws finance jargon at you. 🔖

New term every day. Follow @equivisionbasics.

Educational content only, not financial advice.

#yield #investing #finance #personalfinance #financialliteracy #moneybasics #learnfinance

slides.headline: Yield is [[yearly income]] as a [[percentage]] of an investment's price.
slides.footer: It tells you what an investment pays you.

slides.headline: A bond costs [[$1,000]] and pays $40 a year.
slides.closing: Yearly income as a % of price is [[yield]].

slides.label: PRICE VS YIELD

slides.title: Yield = Income ÷ Price

posts.caption:
Capital gains, explained simply 👇

A capital gain is the profit you make when you sell an asset, like shares, for more than you paid. If you sell for less, it's a capital loss.

Save this for the next time someone throws finance jargon at you. 🔖

New term every day. Follow @equivisionbasics.

Educational content only, not financial advice.

#capitalgains #investing #finance #personalfinance #financialliteracy #moneybasics #learnfinance

slides.headline: A capital gain is the [[profit]] when you [[sell]] something for more than you paid.

visual.arcText: sell for more than you paid

slides.footer: The difference is your gain.

slides.label: ONLY WHEN SOLD
slides.headline: Real once you [[sell]].
slides.sub: Before selling, it's called an unrealized gain.

rows.text: The price is up, but you haven't sold
You sold: the gain is realized

slides.note: Tax rules differ by country and by how long you hold.

slides.label: THE OTHER SIDE
slides.headline: Or a loss.
slides.sub: Sell for less than you paid and it's a capital loss.
slides.note: Illustrative numbers only.

slides.title: Capital gain = Sale profit
slides.sub: Sell higher than you paid.

slides.footer: The mix drives how bumpy the ride is.

slides.label: FIT THE GOAL
slides.headline: The mix fits the [[goal]].
slides.sub: Time until you need the money matters.

rows.text: Years away: can hold more stocks

slides.label: REBALANCING
slides.headline: Keep the mix [[on track]].
slides.sub: Markets move, so your split drifts.

rows.text: Stocks jump: now 70%, not 60%

Back to plan: that's rebalancing

posts.caption:
Recession, explained simply 👇

A recession is a period when the economy shrinks for a while: people spend less, businesses earn less and jobs get harder to find.

Save this for the next time someone throws finance jargon at you. 🔖

New term every day. Follow @equivisionbasics.

Educational content only, not financial advice.

#recession #economy #finance #personalfinance #financialliteracy #moneybasics #learnfinance

slides.headline: A recession is a period when the [[economy shrinks]] and [[jobs]] get harder to find.
slides.footer: It's a broad slump, not one bad day.

slides.headline: How a slowdown can [[build]].
slides.closing: A broad, lasting slump is a [[recession]].

slides.label: A RULE OF THUMB
slides.headline: Two quarters in a [[row]].
slides.sub: Falling output (GDP) twice in a row is a common sign.

rows.text: The economy's output falls
It falls again
Many call that a recession

slides.note: Official definitions vary. Some countries use broader signs.

slides.label: AND THEN?
slides.headline: Recessions [[end]].
slides.sub: They're temporary, but they hurt while they last.

rows.text: Central banks may cut rates to help
Governments can spend to support demand
Unemployment often rises during one

slides.note: Every recession has different causes.

slides.title: Recession = Economic slump
slides.sub: The economy shrinks for a while.

posts.caption:
Central bank, explained simply 👇

A central bank, like the Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank or the Bank of England, manages a country's or region's money, sets key interest rates and keeps the banking system stable.

Save this for the next time someone throws finance jargon at you. 🔖

New term every day. Follow @equivisionbasics.

Educational content only, not financial advice.

#centralbank #economy #finance #personalfinance #financialliteracy #moneybasics #learnfinance

slides.headline: A central bank manages a country's or region's [[money]] and sets [[interest rates]].
slides.footer: Its choices ripple through the whole economy.

slides.headline: Prices are rising [[too fast]].
slides.closing: Its main tool is the [[interest rate]].

slides.label: BOTH WAYS
slides.headline: Rates go both [[ways]].
slides.sub: The bank steers the economy with them.

rows.text: Rates up: slows spending, cools prices
Rates down: cheaper loans, more spending

slides.note: Central banks also watch jobs and financial stability.

slides.label: WHY YOU'LL NOTICE
slides.headline: It reaches your [[wallet]].
slides.sub: Central bank decisions ripple outwards.

rows.text: Loans and mortgages get pricier or cheaper
Savings rates tend to follow
Rates influence how fast prices rise

slides.note: The effect isn't instant. It can take months.

slides.title: Central bank = Rate setter
slides.sub: The bank for the whole country.

posts.caption:
Market cap, explained simply 👇

Market capitalization, or market cap, is a company's share price multiplied by its number of shares. It's the market's price tag for the whole company.

Save this for the next time someone throws finance jargon at you. 🔖

New term every day. Follow @equivisionbasics.

Educational content only, not financial advice.

#marketcap #stocks #finance #personalfinance #financialliteracy #moneybasics #learnfinance

slides.headline: Market cap is the [[share price]] times the [[number of shares]].
slides.footer: It's the market's price tag for the whole company.

slides.headline: A company has 1,000,000 shares at [[$20]] each.
slides.closing: The company's price tag is its [[market cap]].

slides.label: SIZE GROUPS
slides.headline: Small, mid, [[large]].
slides.sub: Investors group companies by market cap.

rows.text: Roughly under $2 billion
Roughly $2 to $10 billion
Roughly over $10 billion

slides.note: Cutoffs vary by source. These are common rough ranges.

slides.label: PRICE ISN'T SIZE
slides.headline: Price isn't size.
slides.sub: A higher share price doesn't mean a bigger company.
slides.note: Illustrative numbers only.

slides.title: Market cap = Price × Shares
slides.sub: The company's price tag.
checks: A cheap share can be a **big company**

posts.caption:
P/E ratio, explained simply 👇

The price-to-earnings ratio, or P/E, is a share's price divided by its yearly profit per share. It shows how much investors pay for each dollar of profit.

Save this for the next time someone throws finance jargon at you. 🔖

New term every day. Follow @equivisionbasics.

Educational content only, not financial advice.

#peratio #stocks #finance #personalfinance #financialliteracy #moneybasics #learnfinance

slides.headline: The P/E ratio is a share's [[price]] divided by its [[yearly profit]] per share.
slides.footer: It shows what investors pay for each $1 of profit.

slides.headline: A share costs [[$50]]. It earned $5 per share.

steps.title: Share price: $50
steps.sub: What you pay for one share.

slides.closing: Investors pay $10 per $1 of profit: [[P/E]] of 10.

slides.label: CHEAP OR PRICEY?
slides.headline: Cheap or pricey?
slides.sub: A higher P/E means paying more for each $1 of profit.

chart.title: Price paid for $1 of yearly profit

slides.note: A higher P/E can mean investors expect faster growth.

slides.label: HANDLE WITH CARE
slides.headline: One number [[isn't enough]].
slides.sub: P/E is a starting point, not a verdict.

rows.text: A low P/E isn't always a bargain
A high P/E isn't always expensive
Compare within the same industry

slides.note: No single ratio tells the whole story.

slides.title: P/E = Price ÷ Profit
slides.sub: How much you pay for $1 of profit.

posts.caption:
Volatility, explained simply 👇

Volatility is how much and how fast a price moves up and down. Calm assets move slowly, while volatile assets swing wildly.

Save this for the next time someone throws finance jargon at you. 🔖

New term every day. Follow @equivisionbasics.

Educational content only, not financial advice.

#volatility #markets #finance #personalfinance #financialliteracy #moneybasics #learnfinance

slides.headline: Volatility is how much and how fast a price [[swings]] up and down.
slides.footer: It measures the ride, not the destination.

slides.headline: Two investments both end the year at [[$100]].
slides.closing: The size of the swings is [[volatility]].

slides.label: READING IT
slides.headline: Low, high, and the [[VIX]].
slides.sub: Volatility can be measured and compared.

rows.text: Small swings, more predictable
Big swings, bigger surprises
A famous 'fear gauge' for US stocks

slides.note: Volatility isn't good or bad. It's how bumpy the ride is.

slides.label: FALLS HURT MORE
slides.headline: Falls hurt more.
slides.sub: You need a bigger gain to recover from a fall.
slides.note: Math: $50 must double to get back to $100.

slides.title: Volatility = Price swings
slides.sub: How bumpy the ride is.
checks: It's about the **ride**, not the result

posts.caption:
Hedging, explained simply 👇

Hedging means taking a second position that gains when your first one loses, to reduce the risk of a big loss. It works a bit like insurance.

Save this for the next time someone throws finance jargon at you. 🔖

New term every day. Follow @equivisionbasics.

Educational content only, not financial advice.

#hedging #risk #finance #personalfinance #financialliteracy #moneybasics #learnfinance

slides.headline: Hedging is a [[second position]] that protects you if your [[first one]] goes wrong.
slides.footer: It limits the damage, but has a cost.

slides.headline: A baker must buy wheat in [[3 months]].

steps.title: The baker agrees a price today
steps.sub: A deal to buy later at a set price.

steps.title: Price rises? Still protected
steps.sub: The baker pays the agreed price.

slides.label: TWO SIDES
slides.headline: Protection has a [[price]].
slides.sub: Like insurance, you may pay for something you don't use.

rows.text: Protects you if things go badly
Costs money or can limit your gains
Best used against a specific, known risk

slides.note: Hedging reduces risk. It doesn't remove it.

slides.label: WHO HEDGES?
slides.headline: Many people [[hedge]].
slides.sub: Businesses and investors both use it.

rows.text: Farmers lock in crop prices
Airlines lock in fuel costs
Even insurance is a kind of hedge

slides.note: Real hedging can be complex. Educational only.

slides.title: Hedge = Protection
slides.sub: A safety net for a possible loss.

posts.caption:
Leverage, explained simply 👇

Leverage means using borrowed money to invest more than you have. It can boost your gains, but it boosts your losses too.

Save this for the next time someone throws finance jargon at you. 🔖

New term every day. Follow @equivisionbasics.

Educational content only, not financial advice.

#leverage #risk #finance #personalfinance #financialliteracy #moneybasics #learnfinance

slides.headline: Leverage is using [[borrowed money]] to invest [[more]] than you have.
slides.footer: It magnifies both gains and losses.

slides.headline: You have [[$1,000]]. A lender adds another $1,000.

slides.label: IT CUTS BOTH WAYS
slides.headline: It cuts both ways.
slides.sub: A 10% rise gives you +20%. A 10% fall costs you 20%.
slides.note: Simplified: ignores interest and fees on the loan.

slides.label: HANDLE WITH CARE
slides.headline: Bigger swings, [[bigger risk]].
slides.sub: Leverage is risky, especially for beginners.

rows.text: You still owe the loan if the price falls
Interest costs eat into your gains
A big fall can wipe out your stake

slides.note: Very risky. Educational only, not a recommendation.

slides.title: Leverage = Borrowed boost
slides.sub: Bigger gains, bigger losses.
checks: The loan must be **repaid** either way

posts.caption:
Options, explained simply 👇

An option is a contract that gives you the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell something at a set price by a set date. You pay a price, the premium, for that right.

Save this for the next time someone throws finance jargon at you. 🔖

New term every day. Follow @equivisionbasics.

Educational content only, not financial advice.

#options #derivatives #finance #personalfinance #financialliteracy #moneybasics #learnfinance

slides.headline: An option gives you the [[right]], not the [[duty]], to buy or sell at a set price.

visual.arcText: the right to buy or sell

slides.footer: You pay a price, the premium, for that right.

slides.headline: A share costs [[$100]]. You think it will rise.

steps.title: You pay $5 for an option
steps.sub: The right to buy at $100 later.

slides.closing: That right to buy is a call [[option]].

slides.label: BEST AND WORST
slides.headline: You know your [[worst case]].
slides.sub: When you buy an option, your loss is capped.

rows.text: Best case: gains can be large
Worst case: you lose the $5 you paid
The option expires on a set date

slides.note: Selling options can carry much bigger risks.

slides.label: TWO FLAVORS
slides.headline: Call or [[put]].
slides.sub: The two basic types of options.

rows.text: The right to buy at a set price
The right to sell at a set price
Options can expire worthless

slides.note: Options are complex. Educational only, not advice.

slides.title: Option = A right, not a duty
slides.sub: You choose whether to use it.
checks: A **contract** with a set price and date
You have the **right**, not the duty

posts.caption:
Short selling, explained simply 👇

Short selling is a way to profit when a price falls: you borrow shares, sell them, and buy them back later, hopefully cheaper. It carries big risks.

Save this for the next time someone throws finance jargon at you. 🔖

New term every day. Follow @equivisionbasics.

Educational content only, not financial advice.

#shortselling #markets #finance #personalfinance #financialliteracy #moneybasics #learnfinance

slides.headline: Short selling is [[borrowing]] shares, [[selling]] them, and buying them back later.
slides.footer: You profit if the price falls.

slides.headline: You think a [[$50]] share will fall.

steps.title: You borrow a share and sell it

slides.closing: Profiting from a fall is [[short selling]].

slides.label: IF YOU'RE WRONG
slides.headline: Losses can grow.
slides.sub: A price can only fall to zero, but it can rise without limit.

chart.title: Profit or loss per share, sold at $50

slides.note: Simplified: ignores fees and borrowing costs.

slides.label: HANDLE WITH CARE
slides.headline: Very [[risky]].
slides.sub: Short selling is one of the riskier moves in investing.

rows.text: Losses have no upper limit
You pay fees to borrow the shares
A sharp rise can force a costly buy-back

slides.note: Not for beginners. Rules differ by country.

slides.title: Short selling = Bet on a fall
slides.sub: Sell first, buy back later.
